Yes, there are passages in the story that involve subtext, and this subtext naturally enriches the story's setting rather than feeling forced. 

On the surface, the story is a straightforward account of a university department dealing with a leaky building and disruptive repairs. However, the subtext provides a sharp commentary on institutional bureaucracy, avoidance of liability, and the neglected state of the humanities in academia. 

This is particularly evident in the dialogue and official communications. When the administration uses sterile euphemisms—calling a missing waterproofing layer "a deficiency in the original building envelope," mold "microbial growth," and chaotic delays a "fluid" schedule—the subtext reveals an institution more concerned with legal liability and image than the health and working conditions of its faculty and students. Similarly, when the consultant tells Vale the air is "within the recommended range" while simultaneously advising her not to spend extended periods near the open wall in her own office, the underlying message is one of absurd contradiction and institutional gaslighting. 

Furthermore, the subtext of Professor Vale teaching a seminar on "narrative and exile" while being displaced from her own office and shouting over construction drills adds a layer of ironic depth. These elements organically build the setting of a modern, bureaucratic university, making the environment feel lived-in, mildly humorous, and deeply authentic.
